question: Planning, the continuous re-adaptation of the labour market and the overall adaptability of the economy are essential elements in ensuring high income in every Member State.

The new demographic landscape coupled with a widespread demand for zero dependence on foreign workers are leading us to look at the economy as a whole and to reassess which jobs and which businesses can be cost-effective, and viable and profitable in the future. It is clear that we need to move away from a labour-intensive economic model to a knowledge-based model.

Obviously, this kind of model needs to be pursued by society as a whole as the basis of the education system. Future generations of Greeks need to gain skills that will allow them to become digital entrepreneurs (production or trade), product designers, programmers – particularly in the field of AI – and they need to gravitate towards the sciences and the productive arts.

It is clear that the limits of certain markets need to be re-examined so that their needs are sufficiently covered without them becoming saturated. Cheap production beyond national borders is only necessary when planning, know-how and ownership remain outside national borders. In view of this, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Are there European tools that can be used to fully re-design the labour market and the economy based on the above terms?
Are there European tools available to introduce AI in the production processes of small and medium-sized Greek businesses?
Through which programmes does it support conferences and campaigns to re-design the economy with a focus on the future?
answer: Artificial Intelligence (AI) offers great opportunities in terms of boosting productivity and efficiency, and optimising resources. While the Commission does not itself develop tools to introduce AI into production processes, it is active on numerous aspects to make it easier for companies to adopt AI. First, the EU makes public funding available.

The EU’s Horizon Europe Framework programme for research and innovation (1) provides funding for research into the development of AI (2), while the Digital Europe Programme seeks to promote deployment of AI (3), opening it up to businesses and public administrations.

Second, in the 2021-2027 programming period, the European Social Fund Plus (ESF+) invests in EU citizens’ up- and reskilling for future labour market needs, including digital skills. About EUR 1.6 billion will be invested in measures targeting education, training and skills in Greece. Moreover, more than EUR 1.

1 billion are available during 2021-2026 through Greece’s recovery and resilience plan (4) to upskill its labour force. Third, the EU helps innovative small and medium-sized enterprises to access private funding. The InvestEU programme (5) will mobilise more than EUR 372 billion of investment through an EU budget guarantee of EUR 26.2 billion. More than 10% of the resources feed into digital goals, including AI.

Fourth, the EU has established a network of European Digital Innovation Hubs (6), which are one-stop shops supporting companies in their digital transformation, including on introducing AI into their processes.
These tools and funding opportunities are available to companies and employees across the EU, including in Greece.
